items.title: Mapping Amyloid Networks in Alzheimer's Disease: A High‐Order Independent Component Analysis Approach to Gray and White Matter Pathology
items.author: Nigar Khasayeva,  Kyle M. Jensen,  Cyrus Eierud,  Helen Petropoulos,  Allan I. Levey,  James Lah,  Ruiyan Luo,  Enrico Premi,  Barbara Borroni,  Jiayu Chen,  Vince D. Calhoun,  Armin Iraji
items.content:
High-order ICA of 716 [F]Florbetapir PET scans revealed fine-grained gray matter (GM) and white matter (WM) networks. These networks outlined a trajectory in which temporoparietal and frontal GM subdomains and WM networks, specifically the posterior corpus callosum, showed changes consistent with early progression from mild cognitive impairment toward Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder marked by gray matter (GM) changes driven by amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. While GM alterations are well documented, spatially distinct patterns of homogeneous Aβ uptake and white matter (WM) involvement remain underexplored. We applied high-order independent component analysis (ICA) to 716 [F]Florbetapir PET scans, identifying 80 GM and 13 WM networks. Diagnostic and cognitive associations were evaluated via statistical modeling. Identified networks delineated a population-level gradient, wherein temporoparietal and frontal subdomains revealed early signs of transitions from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) toward AD. GM networks, including the hippocampal–entorhinal complex and precuneus, and WM networks, including the retrolenticular internal capsule, demonstrated robust associations with cognitive performance. Our findings highlight the utility of high-order ICA in identifying reproducible Aβ networks and the contribution of WM networks, such as the posterior corpus callosum, in the early pathological landscape of AD.

items.title: Explainable Deep Learning Maps Age‐Dependent Differences Between Alzheimer's Disease and Healthy Brain Aging
items.author: Lee J. Yamin,  Galia Avidan,  Tammy Riklin Raviv
items.content:
Brain age gap (BAG) from structural MRI shows strong age dependence in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Separation between cognitively normal (CN), early and late mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD populations is largest in younger adults and declines with age. Explainable AI (XAI) identifies neuroanatomical patterns underlying this age-dependent diagnostic sensitivity.

Deep learning models predict brain age from structural MRI by modeling normative aging patterns in healthy populations. The brain age gap (BAG), that is, the difference between predicted and chronological age, has emerged as a promising biomarker for neurodegenerative diseases. However, nonlinear patterns of brain atrophy challenge the assumption that BAG functions as a uniform biomarker across the lifespan. As most studies do not account for age-dependent modulation, it remains unclear how the overlap between normative and pathological aging patterns affects the diagnostic sensitivity of BAG with advancing age. To address this question, we trained a 3D convolutional neural network ensemble for brain age prediction on a healthy cohort ( = 25,629) and applied it to the ADNI dataset ( = 1203). We characterized how BAG varies as a function of both chronological age and disease stage. Analyses were stratified across the adult lifespan (55–80 years) and disease continuum, including early and late mild cognitive impairment (EMCI and LMCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD). We then used explainable AI (XAI) to identify the neuroanatomical drivers of the observed age-dependent patterns. Our analysis indicated that BAG was an age-sensitive metric exhibiting the most pronounced elevations in younger adults. In AD, BAG attenuated from +8.16 years (55–65 years) to +2.07 years (75–80 years), and significant elevations in EMCI and LMCI were limited to younger cohorts. XAI linked this signal attenuation to two neuroanatomical patterns: a pattern where disease-related differences narrowed with age (most prominently in the hippocampus), and a pattern where normative atrophy exceeded disease-associated changes (most prominently in the lateral ventricles). Consistent with these structural findings, we observed significant age-modulation in the associations between BAG and nine clinical and functional measures. These findings establish BAG as an age-sensitive metric, with the separation between disease and cognitively normal aging greatest in younger adults and diminishing across older age groups, and underscore the importance of interpreting age-dependent regional patterns throughout the lifespan.

items.title: A Data‐Driven Method to Map the Functional Organisation of Human Brain White Matter
items.author: Yifei Sun,  James M. Shine,  Robert D. Sanders,  Robin F. H. Cash,  Sharon L. Naismith,  Fernando Calamante,  Jinglei Lv
items.content:
Using track dynamic functional connectivity, we identify functionally coherent white matter track clusters from multimodal MRI. These clusters exhibit age-related reductions in functional coupling strength and variability and significantly mediate cognitive ageing, revealing the dynamic structural–functional architecture of white matter.

The white matter (WM) of the brain is organised into axonal bundles that support long-range neural communication. Although diffusion MRI (dMRI) enables detailed mapping of these pathways through tractography, how WM pathways directly facilitate large-scale neural synchronisation remains poorly understood. We developed a data-driven framework that integrates dMRI and functional MRI (fMRI) to model the dynamic coupling supported by WM tracks. Specifically, we employed track dynamic functional connectivity (Track-DFC) to characterise functional coupling of remote grey matter connected by individual WM tracks. Using independent component analysis as a Track-DFC feature-extraction step followed by -medoids clustering, we derived functionally coherent clusters of WM tracks from the Human Connectome Project young adult cohort. When applied to the HCP ageing cohort, these clusters exhibited widespread age-related declines in both functional coupling strength and temporal variability. Importantly, specific clusters encompassing pathways linking control, default mode, attention and visual systems significantly mediated the relationship between age and cognitive performance. Together, these findings depict the whole-brain track-level functional organisation of WM tracks and provide a powerful tool to study brain ageing and cognitive decline.

items.title: Whole‐Brain Cell–Cell Interaction Axes Explaining Tissue Vulnerability Across the Neurodegenerative Spectrum
items.author: Veronika Pak,  Joon Hwan Hong,  Tobias Robert Baumeister,  Gleb Bezgin,  Corina Nagy,  Simon Ducharme,  Mahsa Dadar,  Yashar Zeighami,  Yasser Iturria‐Medina
items.content:
Three distinct axes of whole-brain cell–cell interaction explain regional vulnerability to 13 neurodegenerative diseases. Neuron–astrocyte and astrocyte–astrocyte interactions predominantly explain atrophy in subtypes of frontotemporal and Alzheimer's disease, revealing shared and disease-specific molecular mechanisms.

Disrupted cell–cell communication represents a fundamental mechanism underlying neurodegeneration, yet how specific signaling patterns relate to regional brain vulnerability remains poorly understood. Here, we map whole-brain molecular interaction networks and their spatial correspondence with tissue damage across 13 neurodegenerative conditions, including early- and late-onset Alzheimer's disease, presenilin-1 mutations, clinical and pathological subtypes of frontotemporal lobar degeneration, Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. By integrating multiregional single-nucleus and bulk RNA-seq data with curated ligand-receptor interaction databases and structural MRI, we reconstruct over 1000 whole-brain maps of ligand-receptor interactions and quantify their associations with regional atrophy patterns. Multivariate analysis identifies three dominant axes of intercellular communication that explain spatial vulnerability to neurodegeneration. Notably, the first axis involves neuron-astrocyte and astrocyte-astrocyte interactions, explaining atrophy patterns shared by frontotemporal lobar degeneration and Alzheimer's disease subtypes. Two complementary axes explain patterns specific to mutations in PS1 and Parkinson's disease. Importantly, validation in an independent post-mortem cohort ( = 375) confirms that late-onset Alzheimer's disease-associated cell–cell interactions predict observed frontal cortex atrophy. These results establish a systematic framework linking local cellular communication networks to spatial patterns of neurodegeneration, revealing both shared and disease-specific molecular pathways associated with regional brain vulnerability and nominating candidate cell–cell interactions for future mechanistic and therapeutic investigation.

items.title: Addressing Inconsistency in Functional Neuroimaging: A Replicable Data‐Driven Multi‐Scale Functional Atlas for Canonical Brain Networks
items.author: Kyle M. Jensen,  Jessica A. Turner,  Lucina Q. Uddin,  Vince D. Calhoun,  Armin Iraji
items.content:
The NeuroMark multi-scale atlas is highly replicable across individuals, datasets, and studies and serves to establish a common reference space in neuroimaging research. Use of the atlas will help to standardize terminology and methodology in the field of neuroscience and reveal many insights into the brain.

The advent of multiple neuroimaging methodologies has greatly aided in the conceptualization of large-scale functional brain networks in the field of cognitive neuroscience. However, there is inconsistency across studies in both nomenclature and the functional entities being described. There is a need for a unifying framework that standardizes terminology across studies while also bringing analyses and results into the same reference space. Here we improve the accessibility of a previously developed whole-brain template of canonical functional brain networks, expanding it into a powerful atlas, by manually labeling, organizing, and describing these networks with terms familiar to the fields of cognitive and affective neuroscience. These data-driven functional networks were developed by utilizing more than 100,000 resting-state fMRI datasets and are highly replicable across individual subjects and datasets and capture information from multiple spatial scales. The current report seeks to help optimize the utility of this atlas in future neuroimaging analyses by enhancing the comparability and easing the interpretation of new findings. The benefits of this atlas are not limited to future template-based or reference-guided analyses, but also extend to other data-driven neuroimaging approaches across modalities, such as those using blind independent component analysis (ICA). Future studies utilizing this atlas will contribute to greater harmonization and standardization in functional neuroimaging research.

items.title: Neurotransmitter and Transcriptomic Basis of Gray Matter Volume Abnormalities in Alzheimer's Disease: A Meta‐Analysis
items.author: Kuanrong Jian,  Pengfei Zhang,  Haoran Xu,  Wenxiong Liu,  Yuanyuan Li,  Graham J. Kemp,  Qiyong Gong
items.content:
This meta-analysis maps convergent gray matter atrophy in Alzheimer's disease and interprets it across brain networks, neurotransmitter systems, and transcriptomic profiles, highlighting multilevel neurobiological mechanisms underlying AD-related structural degeneration.

Alzheimer's disease (AD), the commonest neurodegenerative disorder, is characterized by progressive cognitive decline. However, much remains unclear about brain morphological alterations in AD and the underlying molecular mechanisms. We conducted a whole-brain voxel-wise meta-analysis using Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images to identify consistent gray matter volume (GMV) alterations in AD. Significant clusters were assigned to AAL regions and Yeo 7 functional networks and further annotated via Neurosynth. Spatial correspondence between the meta-analysis results and 29 neurotransmitter maps was assessed with JuSpace. Transcriptional associations were assessed using Allen Human Brain Atlas data with partial least squares regression and gene enrichment analysis. The meta-analysis included 70 voxel-based morphometry studies, reporting 2628 AD patients and 2508 healthy controls. AD patients had lower GMV than controls in the bilateral hippocampus, bilateral parahippocampal gyrus and bilateral amygdala ( < 0.05, FWE corrected), regions mainly involved in the default mode network, ventral attention network and the limbic network. Sensitivity analyses indicated high robustness, with low heterogeneity. Neurosynth decoding found the regions of lower GMV to be related to emotional processing and facial expression recognition. Neurotransmitter mapping revealed multiple spatial correlations, notably with the dopaminergic and serotonergic systems ( < 0.001, FDR corrected). Genes associated with the lower-GMV regions were enriched mainly in cytoplasmic translation, ribosomal subunits, cadherin-mediated cell adhesion, and ligand-gated ion channel activity. These findings suggest that GMV alterations in AD predominantly affect temporal regions within specific functional networks and are associated with neurotransmitter systems and molecular pathways.

items.title: Electrophysiological “Brain Power” Dissipation: MEG Model‐Dependent Power Estimates and Regional Metabolic Correlates
items.author: Vikram Nathan,  Malte Hoeltershinken,  Eleanor Hill,  Carsten H. Wolters,  Sylvain Baillet
items.content:
We calculate power (P) dissipated by MEG-visible currents, a novel metric distinct from metabolic cost. Sensitivity analyzes and order-of-magnitude checks suggest methodological choices for current and resistance could shift estimates by 1–2 orders of magnitude. We then correlate this dipole P metric against whole-brain oxygen and ketone metabolism maps, revealing spatial correspondences.

The human brain is often described as remarkably energy efficient, with its metabolic power consumption estimated at approximately 20 watts (W). Biophysical models partition this metabolic budget across cellular processes, including neuronal signaling. However, the electrical power dissipated by the synchronized cortical activity measurable with noninvasive electrophysiology remains unknown and should not be equated with total cortical energetic demand. Here, we used magnetoencephalography (MEG) source imaging of resting-state activity to estimate electrical power dissipation in cortical gray matter. Across 30 participants, mean total primary power summed over the modeled cortical source space was 6.6 × 10 W. We interpret this value as an empirical, model-dependent power estimate for the synchronized component of cortical activity accessible to MEG, rather than as an estimate of total cortical power. Targ‑eted sensitivity analyzes and order-of-magnitude checks suggested that the tested methodological choices could shift the estimate by approximately one to two orders of magnitude, but not enough to bridge the gap with metabolic benchmarks. Under a magnitude-based root-mean-squares approximation, finite-element estimates of secondary-current dissipation were approximately 30% of primary power in four central-tendency exemplars. Spatial patterns of MEG-derived power showed associations with PET-derived oxygen metabolism and transcriptomic maps of ketone metabolism, with heterogeneous effects across functional networks. These results define the scope and limitations of MEG-derived electrophysiological power estimates and motivate multiscale models linking synchronized electrical activity to regional metabolism.

items.title: Data‐Driven EEG‐fMRI Fusion: From Multimodal Integration to Latent Neural Inference
items.author: Souvik Phadikar,  Xinhui Li,  Eloy Geenjaar,  Reihaneh Hassanzadeh,  Lei Wu,  Mahshid Fouladivanda,  Brad Baker,  Vince D. Calhoun
items.content:
This in-depth methodological review systematically examines data-driven EEG-fMRI fusion frameworks, including ICA-, CCA-, tensor-, and deep learning-based approaches, highlighting their core assumptions, advantages, limitations, and applications. The review further discusses key challenges, evaluation strategies, and emerging directions to guide selection of appropriate fusion methods for specific neuroscientific and clinical questions.

Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) capture neural dynamics across complementary temporal and spatial scales, but analyzing them jointly is difficult: the two modalities differ in measurement mechanisms, temporal resolution, and neurovascular coupling. EEG-fMRI fusion can be framed as an inverse problem, where the goal is to recover latent neural processes only partially observed through electrophysiological and hemodynamic signals. Here, we review data-driven fusion methods published between 2000 and 2025, focusing on techniques that identify shared neural representations across modalities. We organize methods by fusion strategies (symmetric vs. asymmetric), methodological objectives (factorization vs. translation), and modeling assumptions (linear vs. nonlinear), and discuss evaluation metrics and visualization strategies in current use. A recurring finding is the absence of a universal validation standard and the difficulty of interpreting latent multimodal components. Across neurological, psychiatric, and cognitive applications, EEG-fMRI fusion has revealed distributed network dynamics not accessible through unimodal analyses, though temporal misalignment, noise-induced coupling, and model-dependent interpretation remain persistent challenges. We close by discussing directions including nonlinear modeling, flexible coupling frameworks, and large-scale group-level fusion, and situate the field within a broader view of EEG-fMRI fusion as a problem of latent neural inference.
